explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose
   - This is `gh-ost`, a Go-based command-line tool (an open-source utility) whose sole purpose is triggerless online schema migrations for MySQL.
   - It reads the MySQL binary log, streams change events, applies them to a “ghost” table, and ultimately swaps tables, all without using triggers.

2. Analyze the file structure
   - Top-level directories
     • go/cmd: entrypoint for the CLI (`main.go`)  
     • go/base: support code for context, logging, configuration  
     • go/binlog: parsing and reading MySQL binlog files/streams  
     • go/mysql: connection management and MySQL-specific utilities  
     • go/logic: the core migration engine (streamer, applier, migrator, throttler, hooks)  
     • go/sql: SQL statement builder, parser, encodings  
     • doc: end-user and developer documentation, images  
     • resources/hooks-sample: sample external hook scripts  
     • script: build, test, CI, bootstrap scripts  
   - Config/build/deployment
     • go.mod / go.sum: Go modules  
     • Dockerfile.* and docker-compose.yml: containerized testing and packaging  
     • .github/workflows: CI, linting, replica-tests  

3. Examine the README for additional insights
   - Architecture described in prose and via “gh-ost general flow” diagram (doc/images/gh-ost-general-flow.png)
   - Emphasis on:
     • binlog-based incremental copy  
     • pause-and-resume (throttling)  
     • interactive control over a UNIX socket or TCP  
     • external hooks for custom behavior  

4. How to draw the system-design diagram
   a. Main components
      • CLI Parser & Flag Loader  
      • Configuration & Context Manager  
      • MySQL Connection Manager (master and optional replica)  
      • Binlog Reader (using go/binlog + go/mysql)  
      • Event Streamer (go/logic/streamer)  
      • Row Applier (go/logic/applier)  
      • Throttler (go/logic/throttler)  
      • Migrator / Cut-Over Controller (go/logic/migrator)  
      • Interactive Control Server (UNIX socket or TCP, go/logic/server)  
      • External Hooks Runner (resources/hooks-sample)  
      • SQL Builder & Parser (go/sql)  
      • Ghost Table in MySQL  
      • Original Table in MySQL  
   b. Relationships & data flows
      1. User invokes CLI → flags → context  
      2. Context spawns Connection Manager to MySQL master/replica  
      3. Binlog Reader streams DML events → Event Streamer  
      4. Streamer sends events downstream to Applier  
      5. Applier issues SQL statements (via SQL Builder) to ghost table  
      6. Throttler monitors events, can pause the Streamer/Applier  
      7. Migrator drives phases: create ghost table, copy data, apply events, cut-over  
      8. Cut-over: lock table, replace original with ghost, rename, drop old table  
      9. Interactive Control Server listens for status/control commands → can reconfigure Throttler or trigger cut-over  
     10. Hooks Runner calls out to user-provided scripts at key lifecycle points  
   c. Architectural patterns & principles
      - Pipeline/event-driven: discrete stages (read, stream, apply)  
      - Separation of concerns: CLI vs. core logic vs. IO  
      - Modular Go packages: each logical unit under go/  
      - Asynchronous processing: binlog→stream→apply decoupling  
      - Extensibility: hooks, interactive commands  
   d. Key technologies & frameworks
      - Go 1.15+ (go.mod, vendor)  
      - MySQL protocol & binary log parsing (go/mysql, go/binlog)  
      - Docker for CI and local testing  
      - UNIX socket & net/TCP for control server  

5. Tailoring the diagram to this open-source tool
   - Highlight the pipeline: Binlog Reader → Streamer → Applier → Migrator  
   - Show optional branches (test-on-replica mode vs. real-master mode)  
   - Emphasize ext points: hooks, interactive server  
   - Show two MySQL endpoints: master (or replica) and ghost table co-located on same server  

6. Diagram drawing guidelines for the principal engineer
   - Use distinct shapes/colors:
     • CLI & Config: rectangle (light color)  
     • Pipeline stages: sequential boxes (e.g., blue)  
     • Control server/hook runner: different shape (oval)  
     • MySQL endpoints: cylinder icons (database)  
   - Label every component clearly  
   - Draw arrows showing directional data flow:  
     CLI → ConnMgr → BinlogReader → Streamer → Applier → MySQL(ghost)  
   - Annotate control flows (pause, cut-over) with dashed arrows to Throttler and Migrator  
   - Group related packages under swimlanes or container boundaries (e.g., “go/logic” block)  

7. Emphasize detail and completeness
   - Show the lifecycle phases: initialization, initial copy, event apply, throttling, cut-over  
   - Include external integrations: hook scripts, TCP/UNIX control socket  
   - Indicate where user-configurable flags feed into Context Manager  
   - Don’t omit small but essential parts: SQL builder/parser, default logger, test-on-replica branch  

By following this breakdown and grouping each Go package by its role in the pipeline, you’ll produce a detailed, accurate system-design diagram that captures `gh-ost`’s architecture end-to-end.  
</explanation>
